extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (or advanced undergraduates) studying commutative algebra / algebraic number theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted section of a commutative-algebra textbook (chapter on arbitrary valuation rings) together with solutions to numerous exercises; contains definitions, characterizations, and theorems about valuation rings, valuations, DVRs, integral closure, Krull–Akizuki, and many basic commutative-algebra lemmas and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal local subrings are valuation rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K be a field, S the set of local subrings with fraction field K, ordered by domination. Its maximal elements are the valuation rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Zorn's Lemma: given a chain of local subrings ordered by domination, the union is a local subring; maximality implies for any nonzero x either x in V or 1/x in V, hence V is a valuation ring (and local). (Exercise (26.10), and preceding paragraph.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral closure equals intersection of valuation rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K be a field and R a subring of K. Then the integral closure R' of R in K is the intersection of all valuation rings V of K containing R. Further, if R is local, then the valuation rings V dominating R suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every valuation ring is normal, so V ⊇ R implies V ⊇ R'. For the reverse inclusion: for x not integral over R, construct y=1/x and show 1 ∉ yR[y] so a maximal ideal m of R[y] contains y; use a valuation ring dominating R[y]_m to get a V with x^{-1} in the maximal ideal, hence x ∉ V. (Theorem (26.11) with full proof.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of valuation via value group and valuation map
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a field K, a valuation is a surjective homomorphism v: K^× → Γ to a totally ordered additive abelian group Γ satisfying v(x+y) ≥ min{v(x),v(y)} for x ≠ -y and v(xy)=v(x)+v(y). Defining V = {x ∈ K : v(x) ≥ 0} ∪ {0} yields a valuation ring; conversely, for a valuation ring V the quotient group Γ := K^×/V^× (written additively) is totally ordered and the quotient map v: K^× → Γ is a valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equations (26.12.1) and (26.12.2) give the homomorphism and ultrametric inequality. The equivalence is spelled out: V is a valuation ring iff Γ is totally ordered. Example: DVR corresponds to Γ ≅ Z. (Subsection (26.12) with examples and constructions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation ring criterion: for each nonzero x either x or x^{-1} lies in V
rubrics_metrics.description: A subring V of a field K is a valuation ring iff for every nonzero x ∈ K either x ∈ V or 1/x ∈ V (equivalently V is maximal among local subrings ordered by domination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used both as a defining property and as a consequence of maximality (see proof with Zorn's Lemma). Also used repeatedly to check membership and to deduce local/dominating relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultrametric / min-rule for valuations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a valuation v on K and x,y ∈ K with x ≠ -y, v(x+y) ≥ min{v(x), v(y)}; in particular, if v(x) ≠ v(y) then v(x+y) = min{v(x), v(y)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given in (26.12.2) and Proposition (26.14)(1). Proofs use reduction z = x/y ∈ V and v(z+1) ≥ 0 (or =0 when v(z)>0), then v(x+y) = v(z+1)+v(y). Proposition (26.14)(2) generalizes: if x1+...+xn=0 then the minimal valuation among the xi occurs at least twice.

rubrics_metrics.name: DVR characterization by value group
rubrics_metrics.description: A discrete valuation ring (DVR) V of K is precisely a valuation ring whose value group Γ is isomorphic to Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because every x ∈ K has form u t^n with u ∈ V^× and n ∈ Z; hence Γ ≅ Z. Conversely Γ ≅ Z implies V is a DVR. (Mentioned in examples following (26.12).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of valuation from an ordered group via group algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a totally ordered additive abelian group Γ and a field k, form the group algebra R with basis symbols X^a for a ≥ 0 in Γ, extend multiplication by X^a X^b = X^{a+b}, and define v on nonzero sums by v(∑ r_a X^a) = min{a : r_a ≠ 0}. Extending to the fraction field gives a valuation with value group Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (26.13) constructs many valuations with chosen ordered groups (rationals, reals, lexicographic products, etc.). The valuation ring is R' = {x ∈ R : v(x) ≥ 0}, with prime p = {x : v(x) > 0} and localization R'_p is the valuation ring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean value group implies maximal proper subring
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is a valuation ring whose value group Γ is Archimedean (for any nonzero α,β ∈ Γ there exists n ∈ Z with nα > β), then V is a maximal proper subring of its fraction field K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (26.15). Intuition: Archimedean condition prevents refining valuation subrings between V and K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitely generated ideals in a valuation ring are principal; Noetherian iff DVR
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) In any valuation ring V every finitely generated ideal a is principal. (2) V is Noetherian if and only if V is a DVR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (26.16). (1) is a standard property: ideals are totally ordered so finite-generation forces principal. (2) Noetherian + valuation ring implies 1-dimensional hence DVR; conversely DVR is Noetherian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length inequality for torsion-free modules over 1-dimensional Noetherian domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Let R be 1-dimensional Noetherian domain, K its fraction field, M a torsion-free R-module, x ∈ R nonzero. Then ℓ(R/xR) < ∞ and ℓ(M/xM) ≤ dim_K(M ⊗_R K) · ℓ(R/xR), with equality if M is finitely generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma (26.17) gives the precise inequality and the proof using localization, choosing K-basis for MK, injectivity from torsion-freeness, and additivity of length; equality when M finitely generated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull–Akizuki theorem for 1-dimensional Noetherian domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Let R be a 1-dimensional Noetherian domain with fraction field K, let K' be a finite field extension of K, and let R' be a proper subring of K' containing R. Then R' is also a 1-dimensional Noetherian domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem (26.18). Proof uses a nonzero a' in R', finds a0 ∈ R with relation anx^n+...+a0=0 to show a0 ∈ a'∩R and then the length bounds (26.17) to deduce finite generation of ideals in R', hence Noetherian, and 1-dimensionality follows by analyzing primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization in finite extension is Dedekind
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is a 1-dimensional Noetherian domain (e.g., Dedekind), K its fraction field, K' a finite extension of K, and R' the normalization of R in K', then R' is Dedekind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary (26.19). Because R' is Noetherian and 1-dimensional (Theorem 26.18) and not a field, it satisfies the definition of Dedekind domain (normal, Noetherian, 1-dimensional).

rubrics_metrics.name: DVR property preserved under certain field-extension restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K' / K be a field extension and V' a valuation ring of K' not containing K. Set V := V' ∩ K. Then V is a DVR if and only if V' is a DVR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary (26.20). The value group of V is a subgroup of that of V'; a nonzero subgroup of Z is isomorphic to Z, so V is DVR iff V' is. The converse uses Theorem 26.18 to show V' Noetherian when V is a DVR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) for comaximal ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: If a and b are comaximal ideals (a+b=R) then (a) ab = a ∩ b and (b) R/ab ≅ (R/a) × (R/b). Generalization: pairwise comaximal ideals a1,...,an satisfy R/(∏ ai) ≅ ∏ (R/ai) and intersection equals product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solution to Exercise (1.13) gives proofs: use existence of x∈a, y∈b with x+y=1 to show ab = a∩b, then the natural map R/ab → R/a × R/b is an isomorphism; extend by induction to multiple ideals. Also consequences (comaximality preserved under powers, products, etc.) are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idempotents in Z/n and count of idempotents
rubrics_metrics.description: In Z/p^k (p prime) the only idempotents are 0 and 1. In Z/12 the idempotents are congruent to 0,1,4,9 mod 12. In general, if n = ∏ p_i^{n_i} with distinct primes p_i, then Z/n has 2^N idempotents (each residue class is 0 or 1 mod each p_i^{n_i}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (1.14) uses CRT and the primary case to count idempotents and lists explicit residues in the n=12 example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideals and quotients in product rings
rubrics_metrics.description: If R = R' × R'' and a ⊆ R is an ideal, then a = a' × a'' with a' ⊆ R' and a'' ⊆ R'', and R/a ≅ (R'/a') × (R''/a'').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (1.15) constructs a' := {x' | (x',0) ∈ a} and similarly for a'' and observes components separately; quotient decomposes accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime ideals in polynomial extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is a prime ideal of R then pR[X] and pR[X] + ⟨X⟩ are prime ideals of R[X]. More generally, in R[X1,...,Xn] the ideal ⟨X1 - a1, ..., Xm - am⟩ (or simply ⟨X1,...,Xm⟩ when ai=0) is prime when R is a domain and m ≤ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises (2.10) and (2.11) reduce to the domain case via quotient and use basic facts about polynomial rings over domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturation of multiplicative subsets and union-of-primes description
rubrics_metrics.description: For a multiplicative subset S of R, its saturation S̄ := { x ∈ R | ∃ y ∈ R with xy ∈ S } is multiplicative and saturated; R  ar{S} (complement) equals the union of all primes disjoint from S. A subset S is saturated multiplicative iff its complement is a union of primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises (3.13) and (3.14) develop properties: S ⊆ S̄ and any saturated multiplicative superset containing S contains S̄; R  ar{S} is union of primes p with p ∩ S = ∅; special case S = 1 + a relates to ∪_{p ∈ V(a)} p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nilpotents in Z/n
rubrics_metrics.description: An integer m is nilpotent modulo n iff for some k, m^k ≡ 0 mod n, equivalently iff every prime factor of n divides m. Example: in Z/12 the nilpotents are 0 and 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (3.19) gives the criterion and the explicit example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity into product over minimal primes for reduced rings
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is reduced with finitely many minimal prime ideals p1,...,pn, then the canonical map φ: R → ∏ (R/pi) is injective, and for each i there exists an element in the image with nonzero i-th component and zero elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (3.28) uses that the nilradical is intersection of minimal primes, hence zero, to get injectivity; constructs elements annihilated by all but one minimal prime to realize coordinate-wise nonzero images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation isomorphism Hom(R, M) ≅ M
rubrics_metrics.description: For a ring R and R-module M, the map Hom_R(R,M) → M sending φ ↦ φ(1) is an R-linear isomorphism; inverse sends m ∈ M to (r ↦ rm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (4.3). Standard Yoneda-ish evaluation: Hom(R,M) identified with M via images of 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split exact sequence equivalence to direct sum with concrete maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Given maps between L, M, N, the module M is isomorphic to L ⊕ N with explicit splitting maps iff there exist maps satisfying relations: αβ = 0, αγ = id_N, δγ = 0, δβ = id_L, and βδ + γα = id_M (notation as in exercise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (4.15) gives the precise equalities and constructs the isomorphism and its inverse via φ(m) = (δm, αm) and ψ(ℓ,n)=βℓ + γn.
